2 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2021 / 3 OVERVIEW Preparing for URI’s Future THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship research university and the state’s leading public institu- tion of higher education.
As a land and sea grant institution with global reach, the University of Rhode Island carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of Rhode Island, the United States, and the world.
In all aspects of its work, the University of Rhode Island maintains unshakable commitments to aca- demic freedom and expression, shared governance, diver- sity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many commu- nities of interest.
The University of Rhode Island also devel- ops and maintains partnerships for mutual benefit with Rhode Island College, the Community College of Rhode Island, and other private higher education institutions.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES The Board of Trustees is the University’s governing body charged with oversight of critical academic and administra- tive issues, including appointing the University president, annually setting tuition rates, approving the budget, awarding degrees, and formally approving the awarding of tenure to faculty.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES HIGHLIGHTS New University President The selection process for the new University president was global, comprehensive, rigorous, and inclusive, involving every facet of the University community.
The board orga- nized town hall meetings with all University stakeholders and virtual open forums with presidential candidates.
It conducted a totally virtual search and selected the 12th president of the University.
The board is proud of the open and thorough process that led to the hiring of President Marc Parlange, who has already begun strengthening and expanding the Universi- ty’s research mission, including a University-wide call to develop a culture of scholarship and service, which will improve collaboration and communication across colleges, disciplines, and departments.

Even though he is in his early days as president, President Parlange is focusing on expanding URI’s strengths in oceanography, agriculture, engineering, and the arts, along with the importance of student athletes.
He is expected to deliver a new strategic plan in 2022 that will outline the University’s vision over the next several years, which will be shared with you and Rhode Island leaders.
COVID-19 Operations and Response As with other public boards, our work was conducted remotely and in accordance with executive orders during the pandemic.
At every meeting, the trustees reviewed the University’s response to the pandemic and supported its actions to ensure the health and safety of students, staff, faculty, and visitors to campus.
The board praised the entire University community for its outstanding efforts during the pandemic, resulting in 95 percent vaccination rate and a continued very low positivity rate.
Importantly, the University was able to manage its financial resources quite effectively throughout the crisis, and, unlike many other higher education institutions, URI has come through the pandemic quite well.

Ten-Y ear Strategic Plan The University will engage the entire community and key constituencies in the development of a new Universi- ty-wide, 10-year strategic plan (2022–2032) designed to create a vision for the future and what the University aspires to achieve.
A University-wide Steering Committee will oversee the process, develop key performance indica- tors (KPIs) to measure progress of the goals, and analyze trends, challenges, and opportunities impacting the higher education landscape currently and into the future.
Social Justice, Equity, and Inclusion at URI The board is keenly interested in the advancement of social justice, equity, and inclusion at URI.
In October 2020, the board heard from University leaders on one of URI’s transformational goals for the 21st century—to build a community that values and embraces equity and diversity.
At its January, June, and November board meetings, dis- cussions focused specifically on this issue and how to con- tinue to improve the environment at URI.

At its November 2021 meeting, the board reviewed the results of the “Uni- versity of Rhode Island Assessment of Climate for Learning, Living, and Working, ” URI’s first Campus Climate Survey conducted in spring 2021.
The report provides baseline data on diversity and inclusion and may be used to guide decision-making regarding policies and practices at URI to realize its commitment to an inclusive campus and to insti- tute organizational structures that respond to the needs of its dynamic campus community.
Rhode Island’s Blue Economy The Board of Trustees sees tremendous opportunity in marshalling the research and economic development engines of the University to help drive and grow the Rhode Island economy.
URI has been especially engaged in providing the scientific and technical basis for renewable energy, fisheries and aquaculture, environmental quality, marine and coastal conservation, and management efforts in conjunction with stakeholders and Rhode Island government agencies.

The University and the state of Rhode Island are investing mil- lions of dollars in improvements at the Narragansett Bay Campus, home to URI’s world-renowned Graduate School of Oceanography, to advance its efforts in ocean science.
Rhode Island Workforce Efforts The board is focused on the University’s investment in workforce development opportunities, including continu- ing education/certificate programs, professional develop- ment, the URI Online degree program, and 24/7 learning opportunities.
Polaris MEP , a business unit of the URI Research Foundation, is a manufacturing industry partner for the Governor’s Workforce Board providing competitive manufacturing business improvement programs to grow the state’s manufacturing industry.
Innovate@URI helps entrepreneurs and startups access the vast resources of the University to help grow their ideas and their business, with URI’s Business Engagement Center serving as the front door to industry since 2013.

2 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2022 / 3 OVERVIEW Building the University of the Future UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship research university and the state’s leading public institution of higher education.
As a land- and sea-grant institution with global reach, the University carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of Rhode Island, the United States, and the world.
In all aspects of its work, the University maintains unshakable commitments to academic freedom and expression, shared governance, diversity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many communities of interest.
The University also maintains partnerships for mutual benefit with the state’s two other public institutions— Rhode Island College and Community College of Rhode Island—and other public, private, and nonprofit entities.

UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES The Board of Trustees is the University’s governing body charged with oversight of critical academic and administrative issues, including appointing the University president, annually setting tuition rates, approving the budget, awarding degrees, and formally approving the awarding of tenure to faculty.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES HIGHLIGHTS Approved a new 10-year strategic plan The Board of Trustees unanimously approved the University’s 10-year strategic plan, Focus URI.
The plan outlines a strate- gic vision for the University of Rhode Island for the next decade—articulating the institution’s aspirations and the actions that will be taken to achieve them.
The agile, dynamic plan will necessarily evolve, enabling the University to respond to changes in the state and world, while maintaining a firm commitment to its land- Advanced initiatives to drive Rhode Island’s leadership in the Blue Economy Under the board’s leadership, in partnership with the Gen- eral Assembly and the governor, and with the strong sup- port of Rhode Island voters, the University passed Ques- tion 1 on the November ballot.

The initiative provides a $100 million general obligation bond to revitalize URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus by improving outdated facilities and constructing new facilities to support research and educational programs, ensuring that the state of Rhode Island remains a global leader in the Blue Economy.
The Blue Economy—which includes the defense industry, tour- ism, marine trades, fisheries, and offshore wind—is a criti- cal driver of the state’s economy, generating more than $5 billion every year.
By 2030, that total is projected to double.
A modern URI Bay Campus will help create the innovative jobs critical to Rhode Island’s future.
Welcomed key academic and administrative leaders The board welcomed the appointment of Barbara Wolfe as provost and executive vice president for academic affairs.
Wolfe was appointed by President Parlange after an exten- sive national search and will work closely with stakeholders on advancing the University and implementing the 10-year strategic plan.
Wolfe is a successful scholar, researcher, and educator, who skillfully led the College of Nursing since joining the Uni- versity in 2016.

At the college, she built research strength and raised the level of federal research and training grant funding.
She is an innovative academic administrator with a track record of success and led URI into the U.S.
News and World Report’s Top 50 rankings for master’s nursing education.
She is nationally respected in her field, holding leadership positions in several national associations. and sea-grant missions, institutional vision, and founda- tional values.
The ideas in the plan are intended to unify the community, inspire new ideas and actions, and acceler- ate URI’s exciting forward trajectory.
Development of the plan was led by a diverse steering committee comprised of faculty, staff, students, and community members, and incorporates input from hundreds of stakeholders across all URI campuses and the community.
The plan focuses on four strategic priorities with action items and corresponding key performance indicators to track and measure the plan’s progress.
The four strategic priorities are, “broaden our impact, ” “enhance student achievement, ” “foster an inclusive culture, ” and “power the university of the future. ”

4 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2022 / 5 Celebrated the opening of the Talent Development Achievement House In January, the University opened the Talent Development Achievement House fulfilling an institutional goal of establishing a dedicated residence facility for Talent Development Scholars.
URI’s Talent Development—or TD— program recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds, a majority of whom are scholars of color.
From its first class of 13 students in 1968 to the 1,100 current scholars and more than 4,000 alumni, TD has formed a community of accomplished individuals across the state and around the world.
Approved new degree programs to meet the needs of Rhode Island The board approved several new degree programs in 2022 that meet the demands of students and the needs of the state and citizens of Rhode Island.

The new programs include: • A Bachelor of Science in early childhood education, PK-2, administered online and developed in conjunction with the Community College of Rhode Island, that will give the incumbent workforce of early childhood educators accessible, high-quality, and meaningful pathways toward credential attainment, career advancement, and higher compensation. • A Bachelor of Arts in world language education designed to meet changes in the Rhode Island Department of Education’s credentials for world language instructors in PK-12.
The new program ensures that URI graduates are certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elemen- tary, middle, and secondary education. • A master’s degree in data science offered through URI Online. • A Bachelor of Science in nutrition within the College of Health Sciences.
Approved record financial aid support for students Recognizing the inflationary pressures faced by students and families, the board approved an increase in ins- titutional financial aid for undergraduate and graduate students to more than $140 million—a record high for the University.

The significant investment in URI students and student success ensures that the University will remain among the most affordable flagship state universities in the Northeast.
Made significant investments in the student-athlete experience The board approved strategic investments in intercolle- giate athletics to enrich the overall student-athlete experi- ence and leverage the considerable visibility athletics gen- erates to enhance the national and global reputation of the University.
In March, URI welcomed Archie Miller as men’s basketball head coach.
Miller joined the University after holding head coaching positions at Indiana University, of the Big Ten, and the University of Dayton.
At Dayton, Miller built the Flyers into a perennial Atlantic 10 Conference power, making four NCAA tournament appearances in six seasons.
The University also retained Tammi Reiss as wom- en’s basketball head coach.
Reiss has reinvigorated the women’s basketball program, leading the Rams to 20 wins in a season for the first time in 25 years and setting the program on a course for sustained success.

And, the board approved the addition of women’s lacrosse, adding important athletic opportunities for female students at the University.
Endorsed the University’s first land acknowledgment statement The University worked closely with the Narragansett Tribal Council on several initiatives, including a land acknowledgment.
The acknowledgment represents months of important conversations between the Univer - sity and members of the tribe, and it reads: The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People.
We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous people and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present- day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.
Several additional programs are underway or in develop - ment to continue to strengthen the University’s close partnership with the Narragansett Tribe and support and celebrate the tribe’s culture and traditions.

Formed new board committees to advance research and University facilities The board approved the creation of two new special ad hoc committees: the Sponsored Research Committee and the Real Estate Committee.
These committees are designed to address specific needs of the University and accelerate progress in these priority areas.
Contributed to important legislative changes Members of the board successfully testified in favor of legislation, including a bill that provides the board the flexibility to participate remotely in open public meetings of the board.
The board extends its appreciation to the General Assembly for this key legislative decision that enables the University and board to nimbly and effectively address emerging needs and opportunities.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-01
October 15, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - FOR ACTION
(Introduced at the September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting)
Creates standard process for committee formation
Approved by FSEC 08/31/26 and 10/7/26 (as amended)
Reviewed by CBUM 09/28/26 and 10/8/26 (as amended)
Legislation effective date: Spring semester 2027
Rationale: The limited number of faculty senators, in combination with University-Manual-mandated committee staffing requirements, can make it difficult to staff an expanding number of standing committees. This makes it important to ensure that additional standing committees and subcommittees, whose charges and memberships are proscribed in the University Manual, are created only in response to a significant and sustained need. In contrast, special committees can be created by the Faculty Senate to address pressing issues. While there is no limit to the length of time a special committee can exist, the faculty senate must vote to reauthorize each special committee each year.

This legislation mandates that a newly formed committee must exist as a special committee for at least three (3) years before legislation reconstituting it as a standing committee or subcommittee can be considered by the Faculty Senate. Such legislation must be accompanied by language specifying the charge and membership of the standing committee for inclusion in the University Manual. This change provides time for the Faculty Senate to 1) consider whether a new standing committee or subcommittee is truly warranted; and 2) craft an appropriate and achievable charge for the body.
This legislation does not mandate that a special committee must be reconstituted as a standing committee after three years. It is also not retroactive, i.e., all existing standing committees and subcommittees remain unchanged.
This original version of this legislation was introduced for discussion at the 9/17/26 Faculty Senate meeting. The final version has been revised as follows in response to faculty/staff comments.

1. Remove language mentioning joint committees. Joint committees are, by definition, created in concert with the administration (staffing, wording, charge, power balance). While the faculty and administration may choose to designate a joint committee as a special joint committee subject to the rules and procedures detailed below, the power to do so does not rest exclusively with the faculty senate.
2. Identify the assessment process and who conducts it. Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that the Special Committee’s self-assessment shall be reviewed by FSEC. FSEC which shall use it as the basis for a recommendation to the Faculty Senate to vote on whether the Committee should dissolve, continue as a Special Committee, or be reconstituted as a permanent Standing Committee or Subcommittee.
3. What happens if no reauthorization vote is taken before the end of the AY? Added language to §4.11.1 specifying that all Special Committees are annually authorized by vote of the Faculty Senate. A Special Committee that has not received an affirmative reauthorization vote (assuming that no duly authorized extension has been granted) within one year of authorization shall be dissolved.

4. After the third-year review, can a reauthorized Special Committee apply to change its status? Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that a Special Committee must wait at least two years after its third-year review (i.e., be in its fifth consecutive year of operation) before requesting that the Faculty Senate reconsider reconstituting it as a Standing Committee or Subcommittee.
